title: Carried by memory
hook: for a long time, tradition says, the teaching was memorized and chanted by reciters, not written
carry: the binding of an unwritten book

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangiti, elders reciting the teaching together, question by question. Your line: held by many mouths, not just one memory. Today, what happened to all those words next.
screen: `HELD BY MANY MOUTHS, NOT JUST ONE MEMORY.`

segments.voice: "Thus have I heard." Open the Long Discourses at the beginning and that is how the first sutta starts, and the same words open sutta after sutta. Tradition says the voice is Ananda's, at the council, reciting what he heard the Buddha say. It's a strange way to start a holy text. Not: thus it is. Not: thus it was written. Thus I heard it. The teaching opens by telling you how it reached you: through someone's ears, and someone's memory. Today, how the teaching traveled before it was written down.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `NOT: THUS IT WAS WRITTEN.` → `THROUGH SOMEONE'S EARS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says that after the council, groups of monks took on different collections of the teaching and learned them by heart, chanting them together and teaching them to their students, who taught their own. A text was not a book on a shelf. It was a group of people who could say it. Read the suttas and you notice the repetition: the same passage again and again, lists of three things, four things, eight things, whole paragraphs repeated with one word changed. On paper, that can feel slow. Out loud, it helps a memory hold its shape. Repetition works like the binding of an unwritten book. The Vinaya tells of an elder named Purana who arrived after the council was over. The elders invited him to accept what they had recited. He said it was well recited, but he would remember the teaching the way he himself had heard it from the Buddha. The text records his answer and moves on. Even in the first generation, memory came in more than one voice. At last, the chronicles of Sri Lanka say, in a time of hardship, monks there wrote the texts down so they would not be lost. Until then, tradition says, they had been carried in people. Heard that way, the long stretch before writing looks less like a gap than a kind of care: the teaching was kept alive by being said aloud, by people who had given their lives to it.
screen: `A TEXT WAS A GROUP OF PEOPLE.` · `REPETITION HOLDS THE SHAPE.` · `PURANA KEPT HIS OWN.` · `WRITTEN DOWN AT LAST.` · then, large: `CARRIED BY MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Take today's line, thus have I heard, or a short line of your own from a teaching or a poem you love, and say it aloud three times. Then close your eyes and say it once more without looking; if a word slips, look, and try again.
Reciters. They carried the teaching by memory, chanting it together and passing it on by mouth before it was written. Today's word.
Your line: the binding of an unwritten book. The words lived in people before they lived on a page. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries, monks and novices learn suttas and verses by heart and chant them together, and some monks learn whole collections.

original.note: Pali: thus have I heard. the opening of the suttas, said in Ananda's voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old book someone wrote down.
what it means: a teaching held in people, chanted together and passed from teacher to student.
what a scholar hears: evam me sutam, thus have I heard; the repetition and lists of the suttas fit a text shaped for recitation, and the Sri Lankan chronicles tell of the writing down later.

chat.says: How did the Buddha's teaching survive before anyone wrote it down?
options: Monks learned it by heart and chanted it together, teacher to student.
One monk memorized everything alone and dictated it much later.
It was carved on stone tablets right after the Buddha died.
chat.meaning: Tradition says reciters took on collections, learned them by heart and passed them on aloud, until monks in Sri Lanka wrote them down.

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's attendant, who recited the discourses

Purana.meaning: an elder who kept the teaching as he'd heard it

sources.ref: Dipavamsa 20; Mahavamsa 33 (the texts written down in Sri Lanka)

notes: Quoted: 'Thus have I heard.' as in Rhys Davids, Dialogues of the Buddha (1899). Confirm exact wording.
Outline says 'for centuries'; the claims rule keeps the script to 'for a long time, tradition says' with no number of years. Keeper may restore a span if a cited text supports it.
Reciters (bhanakas) specializing in collections: attested in the commentaries; stated as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Writing down: Dipavamsa 20.20–21 and Mahavamsa 33.100–101 (reign of Vattagamani). No date given on purpose. Confirm references.
'Lists of three things, four things, eight things' are examples of list form, not counts of the canon; confirm acceptable.
howItsDone: 'some monks learn whole collections' (e.g. tipitakadhara examinations in Myanmar); confirm.
Editor pass: the claim that repetition is how memory holds its shape softened to 'helps' (scholarly view, not in the cited text); 'daily' cut from howItsDone.
Audit: unsourced claim about how 'the tradition treats' the oral period, and 'every day', reworded as the script's own reading.
